newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI FINALLY COMES TO TERM WITH OWN BODY.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI FINALLY COMES TO TERM WITH OWN BODY.

text.p: Deborah Compagnoni's biggest opponent in her Alpine skiing career has usually been her own body.
Already the greatest Italian woman Alpine skier of all time and the only one to win gold at consecutive Olympics, Compagnoni's popularity rivals that of compatriot Alberto Tomba.
And the bad news for her rivals at the world championships opening in Sestriere at the weekend is that Compagnoni and her body finally appear to have declared peace.
The 26-year-old started the season without the usual ailments and has won four races since then, more than she has ever captured before in a single season.
More remarkably, she suffered a minor bout of influenza at Zwiesel in Germany this month but still won.
Compagnoni's following in Italy has mushroomed in recent weeks.
"A popular phenomenon has emerged around Deborah that until now had happened only to Alberto Tomba," declared the Gazzetta dello Sport newspaper.
"Debbymania breaks out," said Tuttosport.
An estimated 10,000 fans descended on Cortina d'Ampezzo on Sunday to witness Compagnoni's first World Cup triumph on Italian snow.

After that giant slalom win, her third in a row, Compagnoni was driven at the head of a rowdy motorcade around the town and down usually quiet pedestrian streets with the Italian flag fluttering from car windows.
"They told me 1997 was going to be my year and it seems to be so far," she told Italian television later.
"It all seems a bit easier with these great results."
The headline in the daily Gazzetta dello Sport after Compagnoni pulled off back-to-back wins in two giant slaloms held in the German resort of Zwiesel this month summed up most Italians' feelings.
"Deborah, perfection exists," it said.
The comparisons with Tomba end on the piste for Compagnoni, whose parents run a hotel in the mountain resort of Santa Catarina Valfurva.
The pair trained together in the early years but their temperaments are very different.
"She is a girl who simply pretends to be what she is compared to a braggart who is always a little out of line. She has an ingenuous air while he is the great swashbuckler," said the Gazzetta.
In Sestriere both intend to stick to the same technical disciplines, with Compagnoni hinting heavily that she will not compete in the super-G that she has raced in past years.
At Cortina she skipped the super-G to concentrate on the giant, which has brought her most success this season. She leads the World Cup giant standings after six races.
Although she can compete in the super-G if she wants, Compagnoni also said she felt it would not be fair on other members of the team to deprive them of a place.
"I don't want to take away a place from one of my team mates," she said. "I don't know. We'll see."
In the decade since she started out, the double Olympic champion has kept the medical profession busy.
While Tomba, the showman king of Italian skiing, won race after race, the popularly-acclaimed "Queen" Compagnoni seemed to be forever visiting the specialists.
And while Tomba started the season with 47 World Cup wins, Compagnoni had only seven in a decade marked by success in the big events but plenty of suffering in between.
She has undergone four knee operations, a twisted small intestine that put her in the emergency room for a while and a kidney infection that sidelined her for months.
One day after she won the Olympic super-giant slalom at the Albertville Olympics, Compagnoni ripped a ligament in her left knee in the first run of the slalom.
She had earlier devoted the medal to her doctors.
In 1988, Compagnoni, the junior world giant slalom champion in the previous year, was forced to miss the Calgary Olympics after surgery on her right knee.
She also missed the 1991 world championships in Saalbach, Austria, because of illness.
Compagnoni won the giant slalom gold at the Lillehammer Games in 1994, and then the following summer found while training in Chile that she could barely ski because of pain.
"Her only weakness is her fragility," a former coach said last year at the Sierra Nevada world championships.
This season Compagnoni seems to have overcome her injury jinx while Tomba, by contrast, has been turning his injuries in Bologna.
